    16. Tonelli’s theorem#

    Theorem 15.9 constructed, for measure spaces and , the product measure on the product -algebra , characterized for -finite and by the rectangle formula . In calculus, a double integral over a rectangle is evaluated as an iterated integral: one integrates in with fixed and then integrates the result in . These notes establish the measure-theoretic form of this procedure for non-negative functions.

    Tonelli’s theorem states that for -finite and and for every -measurable function , both iterated integrals of are defined at every point and both equal . No integrability hypothesis is required: the three quantities may equal , and then all three equal . Tonelli’s theorem therefore allows us to compute or estimate an integral on by integrating in whichever order is more convenient. Fubini’s theorem (Theorem 17.1) extends the exchange of the order of integration to functions that change sign; its hypothesis, the finiteness of , is verified by applying Tonelli’s theorem to the non-negative function .

    The proof follows the construction of the integral itself. We verify the theorem for indicator functions of rectangles, extend it to indicator functions of all sets of with Dynkin’s - theorem, pass to simple functions by linearity, and conclude for non-negative measurable functions by monotone convergence.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • State Tonelli’s theorem with its hypotheses (-finiteness, non-negativity, and measurability with respect to ) and its three conclusions.

    • Exchange the order of integration for non-negative integrands, including integrals with value .

    • Prove Tonelli’s theorem for finite measures with Dynkin’s - theorem and monotone convergence, and describe the reduction from -finite to finite measures.

    • Explain with an example why Tonelli’s theorem fails without -finiteness.

    • Prove Minkowski’s integral inequality by testing and Tonelli’s theorem.

    16.1 Statement of Tonelli’s theorem#

    For an -measurable function , the inner integral is defined if the section is -measurable. The outer integral requires, in addition, that be -measurable. This measurability does not follow from the measurability of the individual sections, because combines the values of on all of . Both measurability properties are conclusions of Tonelli’s theorem.

    Theorem 16.1 (Tonelli)#

    For -finite measure spaces and and an -measurable function , the following hold.

    1. For every , the section is -measurable; for every , the section is -measurable.

    2. The functions with values in , are -measurable and -measurable, respectively.

    3. The integral of with respect to equals both iterated integrals: as an equality in .

    All three conclusions hold at every point and for every non-negative measurable ; no exceptional null set appears, and no finiteness of any integral is assumed. The identity (16.2) states that, for non-negative integrands, the order of integration does not affect the value. In particular, if one of the three quantities in (16.2) is finite, so are the other two, and if one of them equals , all three do.

    Remark 16.7 (Measurability of sections)#

    Conclusion (1) does not involve the measures: for every -measurable , all sections and are measurable. The same holds for real-valued , by applying the conclusion to and .

    Warning (Measurable sections do not imply measurability)#

    The converse of Remark 16.7 is false. Let be a set that is not Borel, for example a Vitali set, and let Every section and is empty or consists of one point, so all sections of are Borel sets. But : the map from to is measurable by the measurability of a paired map (Proposition 6.10), and the inverse image of under this map is , which is not a Borel set. Measurability of with respect to is therefore a hypothesis of Tonelli’s theorem that cannot be replaced by measurability of the sections.

    16.5 Minkowski’s integral inequality#

    Minkowski’s inequality bounds the norm of a sum by the sum of the norms. Tonelli’s theorem gives the version in which the sum is replaced by an integral.

    By Tonelli’s theorem, every section is -measurable, so is defined. The function is -measurable and non-negative, so is -measurable by conclusion (2) of Theorem 16.1, and so is its -th root . The function is -measurable by the same conclusion.

    Step 2: testing.

    Let be simple with , where for . The function is non-negative and -measurable. Positive homogeneity, Tonelli’s theorem, and Hölder’s inequality for each give For those with , the bound on the inner integral is trivial. By the testing theorem (Theorem 11.21) on the -finite space , the supremum of the left side over all such is .

    For with counting measure, this is Minkowski’s inequality for non-negative functions. The order of integration is exchanged only after pairing with a test function, because the norm of is not an integral of for .

    Tonelli’s theorem settles the exchange of the order of integration for non-negative integrands on products of -finite measure spaces. Theorem 17.1 extends it to integrands that change sign, where Tonelli’s theorem is used to verify the integrability of .
